outcome: No new upper bound for the exponent of Δ(x) has appeared since 26 January 2024. The best exponent is still the 2023 Li–Yang preprint's θ* ≈ 0.3144831759741, a small step below Huxley's 131/416; the conjectured exponent 1/4 is open. In-window events improve only the lower-bound (Ω) side (Mahatab, April 2025; Lamzouri, May 2026) or treat generalised, smoothed, moment, distributional or effective variants.
problem_asks: Written from the statement, before weighing events. The statement names one case of the Piltz problem: k = 1, so D_1(x) = D(x) = Σ_{n≤x} d(n) and P_1(log x) = log x + 2γ − 1, and the object is Δ(x) = D(x) − x(log x + 2γ − 1). (1) The upper-exponent question: find the infimum of θ such that Δ(x) = O(x^{θ+ε}) for every ε > 0 (the Piltz task 'bounding Δ_k(x)' specialised to k = 1). (2) The conjectured value of that infimum is θ = 1/4 (Hardy–Landau); the bullet does not state it, so it is context, not a part asked for. (3) 'Bounding' in the parent may also cover lower bounds (Ω-results on Δ(x)); the bullet does not say so. Hardy's 1916 result (Δ(x) not O(x^{θ}) for θ < 1/4) is the matching lower-side fact, recorded as context. (4) The bullet asks only for k = 1; no uniformity in k is asked.

events.what_happened: G. H. Hardy (1916) showed that Δ(x) exceeds K·x^{1/4} and falls below −K·x^{1/4} for arbitrarily large x, so the exponent cannot be below 1/4. Known here from the Wikipedia article 'Divisor summatory function' (edited 23 Feb 2026), which gives the date; the 1916 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Lower bound only: Δ(x) is not O(x^{θ}) for any θ < 1/4 (Ω±(x^{1/4})-type). It fixes 1/4 as the least possible exponent and says nothing about the upper exponent.
events.remains: The upper exponent: whether Δ(x) = O(x^{1/4+ε}), the conjecture. Open.
events.direction: Lower-bound side. Consistent with 1/4 being the true exponent; does not bear on whether the upper bound holds.

events.what_happened: Guoduan Mo, arXiv:1105.6155, 'A Proof on Hypothesis of Dirichlet Divisor Problem' (submitted 31 May 2011, one version). The abstract states: 'We have proved that △(X)=X^{1/4+ε(X)}, ε(X)=c/log log X.' The abstract page I opened gives no proof text, so the argument could not be read. A Scribd upload of the preprint is listed in search results; that is not an engagement.
events.delivers: As stated in the abstract: Δ(X) ≤ X^{1/4 + c/loglog X}. Since X^{c/loglog X} = X^{o(1)}, this would give Δ(X) = O(X^{1/4+ε}) for every ε > 0, i.e. the conjectured exponent, if the claim holds. The constant c is not given in the abstract.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim is correct: it would settle the upper exponent at 1/4. The lower side is Hardy's.
events.doubts: No published acceptance, rebuttal or citation found. The 2026 papers I read treat the exponent as open or cite Huxley's 131/416 as the best known (Palojärvi–Tudzi, arXiv:2603.16023, Mar 2026, read to the Theorem 4.6 region; Wikipedia, edited 23 Feb 2026). Neither mentions Mo. The claim is a proof of the widely believed conjecture stated in a single abstract with no readable argument. I did not check the full text.
events.direction: Claims the conjectured upper exponent 1/4 up to a factor X^{o(1)}; if correct, it proves the conjecture.

events.what_happened: M. N. Huxley, 'Exponential sums and lattice points III', Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 87 (2003), 591–609, DOI 10.1112/S0024611503014485, published online 23 Oct 2003. The abstract reduces the lattice-point exponent K to 131/208 and says the divisor-problem exponent becomes K/2 = 131/416. This is the record that Li–Yang (2023) improves on, and the record Wikipedia and the 2026 papers still give.
events.delivers: Δ(x) = O(x^{131/416+ε}), with the log power reported as (log x)^{26947/8320} in secondary sources (not in the abstract I read). Upper bound for the exponent, for the classical divisor problem.

checked_by.who: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication (inferred from publication; no referee report seen).

events.direction: Upper bound: lowers the exponent to 131/416 ≈ 0.31490. Does not reach 1/4.

events.what_happened: J. Bourgain and N. Watt, arXiv:1709.04340, 'Mean square of zeta function, circle problem and divisor problem revisited', v1 posted 13 Sep 2017. Secondary reports (a search summary of the paper, Takeda's paper, and Li–Yang's reference [6]) say its Theorem 2 gives Δ(X) = O(X^{θ+ε}) and the circle error R(X) = O(X^{θ+ε}) with θ = 517/1648 ≈ 0.31371, below Huxley's 131/416. The PDF was binary to my fetch tool, so the theorem number and the value are not checked against the text. v2 (16 Jul 2023) withdraws the paper.
events.revisions: v1 13 Sep 2017 (27 KB). v2 16 Jul 2023 (1 KB), withdrawn.
events.delivers: As claimed in v1 (not verified against the text): Δ(X) = O(X^{517/1648+ε}) for the divisor problem, and the same for the circle problem. The authors have withdrawn the paper, so this is no longer asserted by the authors.
events.time_since_posted: 5 years 10 months to withdrawal (July 2023); 9 years 1 month to 2026
events.doubts: The authors' own withdrawal (v2 comments, verbatim): 'A problem with the proofs of Propositions 2 and 3 (a gap or fault in the reasoning used to claim that the expression in (3.9) is dominated by that in (3.11)); a similar problem with the proof of Proposition 1′ (it is hard to justify the particular application of the Bourgain-Guth reduction theory implicit in a paragraph above Proposition 1′). Theorems 1, 2 and 3 lose their status as theorems.' Not verified: whether the 517/1648 statement is one of Theorems 1–3 (search summaries say Theorem 2). A 2024 Bessel-functions paper (arXiv:2412.14059) is reported, by a search summary, to say BW's first-spacing result fails through a missing positive power of N in their (3.11); I did not find that passage in the text I could read.

withdrawn.what: v2 withdrawal. Notice: 'This paper has been withdrawn by Nigel Watt.' Comments: 'Theorems 1, 2 and 3 lose their status as theorems.'

events.direction: Claimed upper-exponent improvement (517/1648 < 131/416). Withdrawn by the authors.

events.what_happened: Xiaochun Li and Xuerui Yang, arXiv:2308.14859, 'An improvement on Gauss's Circle Problem and Dirichlet's Divisor Problem' (v1 28 Aug 2023; v2 14 Sep 2023; no journal version found). Following Bombieri–Iwaniec, it combines a new first-spacing estimate (Proposition 3.1, proved with small-cap decoupling for a truncated cone, Guth–Maldague) with Huxley's second-spacing results. Theorem 1.2: Δ(X) and R(X) are O_ε(X^{θ*+ε}), with θ* = 0.3144831759741… (Definition 1.1, eq. (1.4)). Conjecture 1.1: θ = 1/4 for both problems. The first-spacing argument uses Bourgain–Watt's double large sieve from their IMRN paper (reference [5], arXiv:1505.04161), not the withdrawn paper. The error-term reductions cite reference [6], which is arXiv:1709.04340v1, in §5 and §7 (eq. (7.7)).
events.delivers: Upper exponent for Δ(X) of θ* ≈ 0.31448, strictly below Huxley's 131/416 ≈ 0.31490; the same exponent for the circle problem. Holds for every ε > 0. The gain is small. Based on the HTML text; the abstract does not state the number.
events.remains: The conjectured 1/4 (Conjecture 1.1), and any exponent between 1/4 and 0.31448.
events.doubts: (i) Dependency on a withdrawn paper: the authors cite arXiv:1709.04340v1 §7 for the error-term reductions and the target bound (5.5) S/H ≲ T^{θ*+ε} is cited as [6, (7.7)]. The withdrawal says Propositions 2, 3 and 1′ of that paper fail and Theorems 1–3 lose their status. Whether (7.7) survives is not known to me. (ii) The first-spacing argument depends on BW's double large sieve from the IMRN paper [5]. A 2024 paper (arXiv:2412.14059, per a search summary) reports a gap in BW's first-spacing result; I did not verify it. (iii) No independent verification found. Citing works (arXiv:2601.01905 v2; a 2025 Preprints.org paper by Runbo Li, seen in snippets only) quote the value without checking it. The 2024 Bessel paper (Guo, Jiang, Wang, Yang) has X. Yang as a co-author, so it is not independent.
events.direction: Upper bound: lowers the exponent from 131/416 to θ* ≈ 0.3144832. Leaves the conjectured 1/4 open.

events.what_happened: Chiara Bellotti and Andrew Yang, arXiv:2303.05028, 'On the generalised Dirichlet divisor problem' (v1 9 Mar 2023; v2 6 Apr 2023). Unconditional bounds for Δ_k(x) for large k, e.g. Δ_k(x) ≪ x^{1−1.889k^{−2/3}} for all sufficiently large fixed k. A search summary reports a 2024 Bull. LMS version; I did not verify it, and the first public date is 2023.
events.delivers: Bounds for the generalised divisor function d_k with large k only (abstract). Says nothing about k = 1.
events.direction: Neighbouring question (generalised k ≥ 3, large k). Does not bear on the k = 1 exponent.

events.what_happened: Timothy Trudgian and Andrew Yang, 'Toward optimal exponent pairs', arXiv:2306.05599 (v1 9 Jun 2023; v2 6 May 2024; v3 15 Jul 2024). A framework for the optimal exponent pair for an objective, applied to ζ in the critical strip, moments of ζ(1/2+it), and the generalised Dirichlet divisor problem. The abstract gives no number for the k = 2 error term. I read the abstract only.
events.revisions: v2 6 May 2024 and v3 15 Jul 2024 are inside the window; I did not compare their contents.
events.delivers: A method for computing exponent pairs and a framework; no classical Δ(x) exponent in the abstract.
events.remains: The classical exponent question, as far as the abstract shows.
events.doubts: Full text not read; a classical k = 2 consequence may sit in the body.
events.direction: Method and framework; neutral to the exponent question.

events.what_happened: Julius L. Shaneson, arXiv:1409.2446, 'Estimates on Lattice Points in the Circle' (8 Sep 2014). Circle problem, not the divisor problem. Gives P(t) = O(t^{1507/4875} log t) in its abstract's terms (b = 1507/4875 ≈ 0.3091, as its abstract states).
events.delivers: Gauss circle problem only. Says nothing about Δ(x).
events.doubts: Its abstract does not mention the 2007 Cappell–Shaneson claim.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (Gauss circle). Not this problem.

events.what_happened: Sylvain E. Cappell and Julius L. Shaneson, arXiv:math/0702613, 'Some Problems in Number Theory I: The Circle Problem' (v1 21 Feb 2007; v2 15 Mar 2007; v3 9 Jul 2007; v4 17 Sep 2014, withdrawn). The 2007 text is reported by a search summary as claiming O(t^{1/4+ε}) for lattice points in a circle. The abstract I opened gives no bound. Circle problem, not the divisor problem.
events.revisions: v1 21 Feb 2007; v2 15 Mar 2007; v3 9 Jul 2007; v4 17 Sep 2014, withdrawn.
events.delivers: Gauss circle problem only (as reported). Not this problem.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by an author: 'This paper has been withdrawn as the authors have not succeeded producing an error free version'.

withdrawn.what: v4 withdrawal (banner: 'This paper has been withdrawn by Julius Shaneson'). Comment: 'This paper has been withdrawn as the authors have not succeeded producing an error free version.'

events.direction: Circle problem; claimed exponent 1/4 in t. Neighbouring problem; no bearing on the divisor exponent.

events.what_happened: T. Makoto Minamide, Yoshio Tanigawa and Nigel Watt, arXiv:2412.11069, 'On the sum of Δ_k(n) in the Piltz divisor problem for k=3 and k=4' (v1 15 Dec 2024), Acta Arithmetica 216 (2024), 291–327, DOI 10.4064/aa230223-28-3. Studies the Dirichlet series of Δ_k(n) and bounds Σ_{n≤x} Δ_3(n) and Σ_{n≤x} Δ_4(n) with Perron's formula. The author name 'Nigel Watt' matches the withdrawing author of arXiv:1709.04340; I did not check that they are the same person.
events.delivers: Averages over n of Δ_3(n) and Δ_4(n). Not Δ_1(x), and not a pointwise bound on Δ_k(x).
events.direction: Neighbouring problem (Piltz with k = 3, 4). Does not bear on k = 1.

events.what_happened: Zhen Guo and Xin Li, arXiv:2410.00936, 'On high power moments of the error term of the Dirichlet divisor function over primes' (1 Oct 2024). Here k (3 ≤ k ≤ 9) is a moment index, not the divisor order. Gives an asymptotic formula for Σ_{p≤x} of k-th power moments of Δ(p).
events.delivers: Asymptotic for prime-restricted power moments of Δ(p), 3 ≤ k ≤ 9. Not a pointwise exponent for Δ(x).
events.direction: Moment asymptotic; neutral to the exponent question.

events.what_happened: Youness Lamzouri, arXiv:2410.03652, 'On the distribution of the error terms in the divisor and circle problems' (4 Oct 2024; math.NT, math.PR). Bounds the discrepancy between the distribution function of Δ(x) and a random model, improving Heath-Brown and Lau. Describes large deviations in a uniform range. Extends to the circle problem.
events.delivers: Distributional statements about Δ(x) (discrepancy and large deviations). No new upper or lower exponent.
events.direction: Distributional; neutral to the exponent.

events.what_happened: Terence Tao, Timothy Trudgian and Andrew Yang, arXiv:2501.16779, 'New exponent pairs, zero density estimates, and zero additive energy estimates: a systematic approach' (28 Jan 2025). Launches the Analytic Number Theory Exponent Database (ANTEDB). The abstract cites four new exponent pairs and zeta-related results. It does not mention Δ(x).
events.delivers: Exponent pairs and zeta-related exponents. No Δ(x) exponent in the abstract.
events.doubts: Full text not read. The ANTEDB divisor-exponent table (blueprint at teorth.github.io/expdb) was not checked.
events.direction: Method and database; neutral to the classical exponent in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Kamalakshya Mahatab, arXiv:2504.17032, 'Omega Results for The Divisor and Circle Problems Using The Resonance Method' (v1 23 Apr 2025; v2 3 Sep 2025, the version read). The resonance method gives Δ(x) = Ω((x log x)^{1/4} (log₂x)^{(3/4)(2^{4/3}−1)} (log₃x)^{−3/8}), improving the log₃ power from −5/8 (Soundararajan's Ω-bound, as cited in the paper). Also Ω-results for the Piltz problem and the circle problem.
events.delivers: Lower bound (Ω) on Δ(x): sharper log₃ power than before. No upper bound.
events.remains: The upper exponent (131/416 vs θ* vs conjectured 1/4) is untouched. The lower-side exponent 1/4 is unchanged.
events.doubts: The only engagement I found is Lamzouri's May 2026 sharpening (arXiv:2605.21476), which improves it; that is building on it, not checking it.
events.direction: Lower-bound side. Consistent with the conjectured 1/4.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, 'On the Generalized Dirichlet Divisor Problem', Preprints.org manuscript 202505.1432 (posted May 2025; v3 Sept 2025). Per search snippets, not the page: gives better upper bounds for α_k for 9 ≤ k ≤ 20, a minor improvement on Trudgian and Yang, and lists the best known α₂ ≤ 0.3144831759741 attributed to Li and Yang. The page returned HTTP 403 to my fetcher; the description is from snippets.
events.revisions: v2 and v3 (Sept 2025) seen in search results; contents not compared.
events.delivers: Generalised problem for 9 ≤ k ≤ 20. Restates the Li–Yang value for k = 2 as a citation only.
events.doubts: Not opened; claims are from search snippets.
events.direction: Neighbouring question (generalised k ≥ 9). Quotes Li–Yang for k = 2 without checking it.

events.what_happened: Sebastian Tudzi, arXiv:2506.21823, 'On the Generalised Divisor Problem' (v1 26 Jun 2025; v2 20 Feb 2026). Dirichlet convolution method for T_k(x) = Σ d_k(n) with k ≥ 3. The v2 abstract page gives |Δ_3(x)| < 2.968 x^{2/3} log^{1/3} x for x ≥ 2, and an order-of-magnitude result for k > 3. A search summary of an earlier version gave 3.369; not reconciled.
events.revisions: v1 26 Jun 2025; v2 20 Feb 2026 (changes not compared).
events.delivers: Explicit bounds for d_k with k ≥ 3. Says nothing for k = 2 (the classical Δ(x)).
events.doubts: Constant for k = 3 differs between the v2 abstract page (2.968) and a search summary (3.369); not reconciled.
events.direction: Neighbouring question (k ≥ 3). Not the classical problem.

events.what_happened: Olivier Bordellès and Florian Daval, arXiv:2601.01905, 'On a Smoothed Dirichlet Divisor Problem' (v1 5 Jan 2026; v2 11 Jan 2026; v3 26 Jun 2026). For the smoothed sum Σ_{n≤x} τ(n)(1 − x/n), gives Σ − xP(log x) = 1/4 + O(log x / x^{1/4}), with P a polynomial of degree 2. As a corollary, settles a conjecture of Berkane, Bordellès and Ramaré on the positivity of an integral of the error term. The v2 HTML also cites Li–Yang for Σ_{n≤√x} ψ(x/n) ≪ x^{θ+ε} with θ ≈ 0.31448, calling it a slight improvement on Huxley.
events.revisions: v1 5 Jan 2026; v2 11 Jan 2026; v3 26 Jun 2026 (the version I read).
events.delivers: A smoothed-weight divisor sum (weight 1 − x/n). Its constant term 1/4 is a constant, not the exponent of Δ(x). Says nothing about the classical upper exponent.
events.remains: The classical Δ(x) upper exponent, and the conjecture.
events.doubts: The v3 page says the work is 'entirely explicit' and settles the Berkane–Bordellès–Ramaré conjecture; I did not check the proof. Its citation of Li–Yang is a quotation, not a verification.
events.direction: Smoothed variant; neutral to the classical exponent. Its citation of Li–Yang is the 2026 citation that treats θ ≈ 0.31448 as the record.

events.what_happened: Neea Palojärvi and Sebastian Tudzi, arXiv:2603.16023, 'Explicit and Effective Estimates for the error term in the Generalised Divisor Problem' (17 Mar 2026). Effective estimates for Δ_k(x) for all k ≥ 2 and completely explicit ones for 3 ≤ k ≤ 9. Theorem 4.6, as read, gives an exponent of 1/2 at k = 2, so no improvement. The introduction cites Huxley's 131/416 as the best known for k = 2 and does not cite Li–Yang in the part I read (about 100k of 167k characters).
events.revisions: v1 only, as far as I could see.
events.delivers: Effective bounds for Δ_k with k ≥ 2 (constants not fixed in the part I read). For k = 2, no exponent below 1/2 in the part read, and no improvement on 131/416.
events.direction: Generalised and explicit; neutral to the classical exponent.

events.what_happened: Youness Lamzouri, arXiv:2605.21476, 'Sharp omega results for the divisor and circle problems' (20 May 2026, one version). Proves Ω-results believed sharp for both problems and determines the sign of the large values. Improves Soundararajan, Sourmelidis and Mahatab, and gives the first improvement on Hafner's 1981 Ω₊ result for the divisor problem. The main tool is a resonance method working with the phase in Voronoï's summation formula.
events.delivers: Lower-bound (Ω and Ω±) results for Δ(x), sharper than before. No upper exponent.
events.remains: The upper exponent and the conjecture (1/4).
events.doubts: Abstract page only; full text not read. Preprint.
events.direction: Lower-bound side. Consistent with 1/4 being the true order.

disputes.summary: Li–Yang (arXiv:2308.14859) cites Bourgain–Watt arXiv:1709.04340v1 §7 for its error-term reductions and eq. (7.7). The authors of 1709.04340 withdrew it in July 2023 and state that its Theorems 1–3 'lose their status as theorems'. No source I read reconciles the two. Li–Yang's first-spacing argument cites Bourgain–Watt's IMRN paper (reference [5], arXiv:1505.04161), not the withdrawn paper.

Sources in 2026 disagree on the current classical record. Bordellès–Daval v2 (Jan–Jun 2026) calls Li–Yang's θ ≈ 0.31448 a slight improvement on Huxley's record. Palojärvi–Tudzi (Mar 2026, the part I read) and Wikipedia (edited 23 Feb 2026) still give Huxley's 131/416 as the best known. Bourgain–Watt's 517/1648 appears only in secondary citations and is withdrawn.

summary: I ran 39 web searches and opened the following: Wikipedia's 'Divisor summatory function' article, arXiv abstract and HTML pages for each event, the Cambridge page for Huxley 2003, and some trackers and databases. The PDFs of 1709.04340 and 2308.14859 were binary to my fetch tool, so Li–Yang's Theorem 1.2 and Conjecture 1.1 come from the HTML text, and Bourgain–Watt's Theorem 2 (517/1648) comes from search summaries and secondary citations. The classical exponent record is Li–Yang's preprint arXiv:2308.14859 (28 Aug 2023): θ* = 0.3144831759741 against Huxley's 131/416 (2003), with Conjecture 1.1 (θ = 1/4) still open. It predates the window. Its error-term reductions cite Bourgain–Watt's withdrawn arXiv:1709.04340v1, so the θ* value depends on a withdrawn paper unless (7.7) is unaffected; I could not check that. Within the window, nothing lowers the upper exponent. Mahatab (April 2025) and Lamzouri (May 2026) improve Ω lower bounds; Lamzouri (Oct 2024) gives distributional results; Tudzi (k ≥ 3), Bordellès–Daval (smoothed), Palojärvi–Tudzi (effective, k ≥ 2, with Theorem 4.6 giving exponent 1/2 at k = 2), Guo–Li (prime-restricted moments), Minamide–Tanigawa–Watt (k = 3, 4) and Tao–Trudgian–Yang (ANTEDB, exponent pairs) are generalised, smoothed or neighbouring variants. Close calls: (a) whether θ* ≈ 0.31448 is 'the' record: Bordellès–Daval (2026) and Runbo Li's preprint (2025, snippet only) treat it as the record; Palojärvi–Tudzi and Wikipedia still cite 131/416; (b) whether the Ω-results count under 'bounding': they bound from below only; (c) whether Li–Yang's dependency on the withdrawn paper invalidates θ*. Mo (2011, arXiv:1105.6155) claims Δ(X) = X^{1/4+c/log log X}, which would settle the conjecture if correct; no engagement found, and the claimed argument was not readable. AI: no source for this problem names an AI system. I searched for AI involvement in the divisor problem through AlphaEvolve, OpenAI (Astra), Anthropic (Claude, Fable), Google (Aletheia), Tao's AI-contributions wiki, Epoch's FrontierMath open problems, the Breakthrough Tracker and Lean/Mathlib. The AI results I found concern other problems (Erdős problems, unit distance, prime gaps, zeta zeros, the divisor function of n!). I read only part of the wiki, tracker and Epoch pages, so unseen entries cannot be ruled out.
competing_reading: One reading: Li–Yang's θ* is the live record and Huxley's 131/416 is superseded, with Bourgain–Watt's 517/1648 as an earlier, withdrawn step; on this reading the in-window events are variants and lower bounds, and the upper exponent last moved in August 2023. The other reading: θ* rests on the withdrawn §7 of arXiv:1709.04340 and has not been independently checked, so the record is Huxley's 131/416 (which Palojärvi–Tudzi and Wikipedia still cite). A further reading: the Ω-results of Mahatab and Lamzouri 'bound' Δ(x) in the problem's sense, so in-window activity is larger than an upper-exponent reading suggests. Mo (2011) is a third reading: a claimed proof of the conjecture that nobody has engaged with.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Li–Yang (arXiv:2308.14859, the §5 and §7 passages and eq. (7.7)), and whether (7.7) is among the withdrawn Propositions 1′, 2, 3 of arXiv:1709.04340; (2) a readable copy of 1709.04340v1 to confirm Theorem 2's statement and whether it is 517/1648; (3) the 2024 Bessel-functions paper's passage on Bourgain–Watt's (3.11) (arXiv:2412.14059, Section 6 or 3); (4) a journal version or a referee report for Li–Yang; (5) a text for Mo's 2011 argument and any reaction to it; (6) the ANTEDB divisor table (teorth.github.io/expdb/blueprint) and the Runbo Li preprint, which my fetcher could not reach (HTTP 403).

event.what_happened: Kamalakshya Mahatab, arXiv:2504.17032, 'Omega Results for The Divisor and Circle Problems Using The Resonance Method' (v1 23 Apr 2025; v2 3 Sep 2025, the version read). The resonance method gives Δ(x) = Ω((x log x)^{1/4} (log₂x)^{(3/4)(2^{4/3}−1)} (log₃x)^{−3/8}), improving the log₃ power from −5/8 (Soundararajan's Ω-bound, as cited in the paper). Also Ω-results for the Piltz problem and the circle problem.
event.delivers: Lower bound (Ω) on Δ(x): sharper log₃ power than before. No upper bound.
event.remains: The upper exponent (131/416 vs θ* vs conjectured 1/4) is untouched. The lower-side exponent 1/4 is unchanged.
event.doubts: The only engagement I found is Lamzouri's May 2026 sharpening (arXiv:2605.21476), which improves it; that is building on it, not checking it.
event.direction: Lower-bound side. Consistent with the conjectured 1/4.

events.credibility_reason: A claimed proof of a landmark conjecture with no engagement, acceptance or citation in 15 years; later papers (2026) still treat the exponent as open and cite Huxley or Li–Yang without mentioning it; single short v1 with no readable argument.
events.direction: confirmed

events.credibility_reason: Withdrawn by the authors in July 2023, who identified specific gaps in Propositions 1′, 2 and 3 and state that Theorems 1–3 lose their status as theorems.

Its error-term reductions cite §7 / eq. (7.7) of the withdrawn Bourgain–Watt arXiv:1709.04340v1, and no source reconciles this; some 2026 sources still cite Huxley's 131/416 as the record. Established authors with a serious method, so kept.
Withdrawn by an author: 'the authors have not succeeded producing an error free version'.

judgement.why: The statement asks to bound Δ(x) for the classical divisor problem (named k = 1 in the list's indexing), with the true order open. No in-window event moves the upper exponent; Huxley (2003, journal) and Li–Yang (Aug 2023, doubtful over its reliance on the withdrawn Bourgain–Watt §7) are pre-snapshot bounds, and Bourgain–Watt is knocked down by its own withdrawal. The close call is the Ω-results of Mahatab (Apr 2025) and Lamzouri (May 2026): they sharpen the lower bound on the size of Δ(x) by log factors, a quantity on the still-open question of Δ's true order, and the parent statement asks for 'bounding' Δ, so I scored them `bound` rather than `variant`; the alternative reading (only the upper exponent counts) would make them variants. Generalised-k, smoothed, moment, distributional, effective and circle-problem papers are variants; method/database papers are none. Mo (2011) claims the whole conjecture but meets several F10 signals (15 years of silence on a landmark claim, later papers still calling it open without citing it) and is set aside. No AI involvement anywhere.
judgement.doubts: The statement's 'k = 1' indexing differs from the usual convention (the classical problem is usually k = 2); I read it as the classical Δ(x). Whether Ω-type log-factor refinements count as moving the problem is a judgement call; if only the upper exponent counts, Mahatab and Lamzouri 2026 should be variants. Li–Yang's dependency on the withdrawn Bourgain–Watt paper is unresolved in the record.
